title: Vancomycin: Infusion and Kidney Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: IV vancomycin requires renal-aware dosing and therapeutic monitoring according to the indication and institutional protocol. Flushing, erythema, pruritus, or hypotension during a rapid infusion may represent a rate-related infusion reaction; stop/slow per protocol and assess for true anaphylaxis.
recognize: Kidney injury risk rises with high exposure, preexisting renal dysfunction, dehydration, and other nephrotoxic drugs.
Infusion reaction is related to histamine release and is not automatically an IgE allergy.
priorities: Verify renal function and ordered monitoring before/through therapy.
Infuse over the prescribed duration and never give IV vancomycin as a rapid IV push.
Assess immediately for airway swelling, wheeze, hypotension, or generalized urticaria suggesting anaphylaxis.
assessMonitor: Trend creatinine, urine output, therapeutic drug monitoring when ordered, infusion site, rash, blood pressure, and response to infection treatment.
interventions: Use pump-controlled infusion and appropriate dilution per product/facility protocol.
If a rate-related reaction occurs, follow orders for interruption, slower restart, and antihistamine treatment when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Concurrent nephrotoxins increase kidney risk.
Oral vancomycin and IV vancomycin are not interchangeable for their common indications because oral drug has minimal systemic absorption.
teaching: Report rash, decreased urine, hearing changes, or severe diarrhea and complete therapy as prescribed.
delegationScope: IV medication administration scope varies by state for LPN/LVN practice; assessment of reactions and renal deterioration requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Documenting a vancomycin infusion reaction as a permanent allergy without assessing whether it was rate-related.
oneLinePearl: Vancomycin safety = kidneys, exposure, and infusion rate.

title: Aminoglycosides: Kidneys and Ears
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin can cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Dose/interval depend strongly on renal function, and drug levels may be ordered based on the regimen; report reduced urine output, rising creatinine, tinnitus, hearing loss, vertigo, or balance changes.
recognize: Toxicity risk increases with renal impairment, prolonged therapy, high exposure, dehydration, and concurrent nephrotoxic/ototoxic drugs.
Vestibular toxicity may present as dizziness, oscillopsia, or gait instability before obvious hearing loss.
priorities: Verify renal function and dosing schedule.
Obtain ordered drug levels at the correct protocol-defined time.
Report auditory/vestibular or renal changes promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend creatinine, urine output, hydration, hearing/balance symptoms, and therapeutic levels when ordered.
interventions: Maintain appropriate hydration when clinically suitable and avoid scheduling errors that invalidate drug-level interpretation.
medicationSafety: Concurrent loop diuretics or other nephrotoxic drugs may increase toxicity risk.
Do not interpret aminoglycoside levels without knowing whether the sample was intended as a peak, trough, or other protocol-specific concentration.
teaching: Report new ringing in ears, hearing change, dizziness, or reduced urination immediately.
delegationScope: Monitoring data may be collected by team members, but toxicity assessment and medication decisions require licensed-nurse/provider review.
examTrap: Giving the next dose without checking a clearly abnormal renal trend or required level.
oneLinePearl: Aminoglycosides can injure kidneys and cranial nerve VIII.

title: Beta Blockers: Rate, Pressure, and Withdrawal
bottomLine: Beta blockers reduce sympathetic effects and may lower heart rate and blood pressure. Assess ordered hold parameters and symptoms, and never abruptly stop chronic beta-blocker therapy without a plan because rebound tachycardia, hypertension, or ischemia can occur.
recognize: Expected effects can include lower pulse/BP and fatigue.
Some beta blockers can mask adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia such as tremor or palpitations.
priorities: Check pulse, BP, and symptoms before administration according to the order.
Report symptomatic bradycardia, hypotension, syncope, or worsening heart failure signs.
Teach gradual position changes.
assessMonitor: Trend heart rate, BP, dizziness, fatigue, weight/edema in heart failure, and glucose awareness in diabetes.
interventions: Use fall precautions when orthostasis or bradycardia is present.
medicationSafety: Nonselective beta blockers can worsen bronchospasm in susceptible patients.
Combining AV-node-slowing drugs can increase bradycardia/heart block risk.
teaching: Do not stop suddenly; monitor pulse/BP as instructed and report fainting or severe breathing problems.
delegationScope: Medication administration follows state/facility scope; abnormal assessment findings require licensed-nurse/provider review before proceeding.
examTrap: Holding or giving solely from one number without considering the actual ordered parameters and symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Beta blockers slow the system—rate, pressure, lungs, and glucose awareness matter.

title: ACE Inhibitors: Pressure, Potassium, Kidneys
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: ACE inhibitors can lower blood pressure and protect selected cardiovascular/renal patients but may cause hyperkalemia, creatinine rise, cough, hypotension, and rare angioedema. Angioedema involving tongue/lips/airway is an emergency.
recognize: A dry cough can occur and is not the same as angioedema.
Potassium can rise, especially with renal impairment, potassium supplements, mineralocorticoid antagonists, or potassium-sparing diuretics.
priorities: Check BP and ordered renal/potassium monitoring.
Escalate facial, tongue, or throat swelling immediately.
Review pregnancy status/potential because ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, creatinine/eGFR, potassium, dizziness, cough, edema, and symptoms of angioedema.
interventions: Teach slow position changes and avoidance of unsupervised potassium salt substitutes when hyperkalemia risk exists.
medicationSafety: Avoid ACE inhibitor use during pregnancy.
NSAIDs, dehydration, and renal artery disease can increase kidney risk in susceptible patients.
teaching: Report facial swelling immediately and do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes unless approved.
delegationScope: Abnormal BP, potassium, renal trends, or angioedema require licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Treating ACE-inhibitor angioedema like a harmless medication cough.
oneLinePearl: ACE inhibitor safety: airway, potassium, kidneys, pregnancy.

title: Loop Diuretics: Volume and Electrolytes
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Loop diuretics such as furosemide remove sodium and water but can cause dehydration, hypotension, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and renal dysfunction. Daily weights and clinical congestion are often more informative than isolated urine output alone.
recognize: Effective diuresis may reduce edema, crackles, orthopnea, and weight.
Dizziness, dry mucosa, hypotension, muscle weakness/cramps, or dysrhythmia can signal overdiuresis/electrolyte loss.
priorities: Assess BP, volume status, weight trend, edema, lungs, and ordered electrolytes/renal function.
Administer at a time that reduces unnecessary nocturia when clinically appropriate.
Use fall precautions when orthostasis is present.
assessMonitor: Trend weight under consistent conditions, intake/output, potassium, magnesium, sodium, creatinine, BP, and symptoms.
interventions: Replace electrolytes only as ordered and based on laboratory/clinical context.
medicationSafety: Rapid/high-dose IV administration can increase ototoxicity risk.
Digoxin toxicity risk can rise when loop-diuretic-induced hypokalemia occurs.
redFlags: Sudden hearing change during high-dose IV therapy
teaching: Track daily weight if instructed and report rapid changes, dizziness, severe weakness, or reduced urine output.
delegationScope: Daily weights and intake/output may be delegated with standardized technique; interpretation of changes remains a licensed-nurse responsibility.
examTrap: Celebrating large urine output while ignoring hypotension, kidney injury, or falling potassium.
oneLinePearl: Diuresis is only successful if congestion improves without draining pressure, kidneys, or electrolytes.

title: Systemic Corticosteroids: Glucose, Infection, Tapering
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Systemic corticosteroids can suppress inflammation but also raise glucose, increase infection risk, alter mood/sleep, cause fluid retention, weaken bone with long exposure, and suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Long-term therapy must not be stopped abruptly without a taper plan.
recognize: Hyperglycemia may appear even in patients without known diabetes.
Infection signs can be muted by immunosuppression.
priorities: Monitor glucose and infection risk according to dose/duration and patient risk.
Administer with food when appropriate to reduce GI upset.
Verify taper instructions after prolonged therapy.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose, BP/edema, weight, mood/sleep, infection signs, GI symptoms, and bone risk with prolonged use.
interventions: Support calcium/vitamin D and bone-protection plans when ordered for long-term therapy.
medicationSafety: Abrupt withdrawal after significant prolonged exposure can precipitate adrenal insufficiency.
Live vaccines may be contraindicated during certain degrees of immunosuppression; follow current immunization guidance.
teaching: Do not stop long-term steroids suddenly; carry medication information and report infection exposure or severe illness.
delegationScope: Medication effects and taper safety require licensed-nurse/provider oversight.
examTrap: Stopping chronic prednisone suddenly because symptoms improved.
oneLinePearl: Steroids calm inflammation but raise glucose, hide infection, and may need a taper.

title: Lithium: Salt, Water, Kidneys, Toxicity
bottomLine: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window and is cleared by the kidneys. Dehydration, sodium depletion, renal impairment, and interacting drugs can raise lithium levels; new coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, vomiting/diarrhea, slurred speech, or severe weakness requires urgent toxicity evaluation.
recognize: Fine tremor, thirst, and mild GI symptoms may occur at therapeutic use but worsening neurologic/GI symptoms are concerning.
NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and some diuretics can increase lithium concentrations.
priorities: Maintain consistent fluid and sodium intake unless another condition requires a specific plan.
Obtain ordered lithium levels at the protocol-defined time relative to the dose.
Hold and escalate suspected toxicity according to orders/policy.
assessMonitor: Trend lithium concentration, renal function, thyroid function, sodium, hydration, tremor, gait, cognition, and GI symptoms.
interventions: Teach sick-day and dehydration precautions and medication-interaction review.
medicationSafety: Do not start OTC NSAIDs without checking for interaction.
Pregnancy requires specialist risk-benefit management; do not independently stop treatment.
teaching: Keep salt/fluid intake consistent and call during significant vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or dehydration.
delegationScope: Toxicity assessment and interpretation of serum levels remain licensed clinical responsibilities.
examTrap: Telling a patient taking lithium to aggressively restrict dietary sodium.
oneLinePearl: Lithium follows water and sodium—dehydration can turn treatment into toxicity.

title: Phenytoin: Levels, Gums, and IV Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Phenytoin has nonlinear pharmacokinetics, many interactions, and a narrow therapeutic range. Toxicity often presents with nystagmus, ataxia, slurred speech, or confusion; IV administration requires cardiac/BP monitoring and strict compatibility/rate precautions.
recognize: Gingival overgrowth is a chronic adverse effect reduced by good oral hygiene.
Low albumin or kidney disease can alter interpretation of total phenytoin concentrations.
priorities: Monitor seizure control and toxicity symptoms.
Use ordered serum levels when clinically indicated and interpret in context.
For IV administration, follow product-specific rate, compatibility, and monitoring requirements.
assessMonitor: Trend gait, speech, nystagmus, cognition, rash, CBC/liver tests when ordered, oral health, and medication interactions.
interventions: Encourage meticulous dental hygiene and regular dental care.
Use consistent formulation/manufacturer guidance as directed because bioavailability may vary.
medicationSafety: Serious rash can indicate SJS/TEN and requires urgent evaluation.
Abrupt anticonvulsant discontinuation can precipitate seizures.
redFlags: New severe rash or mucosal lesions
Hypotension or dysrhythmia during IV administration
teaching: Do not stop suddenly; report rash and maintain oral hygiene.
delegationScope: IV antiepileptic administration scope varies by state/facility; toxicity assessment requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Stopping phenytoin abruptly because the patient has been seizure-free.
oneLinePearl: Phenytoin toxicity walks and talks funny—ataxia, nystagmus, slurred speech.

title: Chemotherapy: Exposure and Extravasation Safety
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Antineoplastic drugs can injure patients and healthcare workers. Administration and spill/waste handling require hazardous-drug precautions; pain, burning, swelling, or loss of blood return during vesicant infusion can signal extravasation and requires immediate protocol-based action.
recognize: Hazardous-drug exposure can occur through skin contact, inhalation, ingestion, or sharps injury.
Extravasation can cause tissue necrosis with certain vesicants.
priorities: Use required PPE and closed-system/engineering controls where applicable.
For suspected extravasation, stop the infusion without automatically removing the catheter until the drug-specific protocol is followed; aspiration/antidote steps may use that access.
Notify the oncology team/pharmacy promptly.
assessMonitor: Inspect infusion site, ask about burning/pain, assess blood return according to protocol, and monitor blood counts/organ toxicity relevant to the regimen.
interventions: Follow drug-specific warm/cold compress and antidote protocols rather than a single universal extravasation treatment.
medicationSafety: Independent double checks and dose verification follow oncology policy.
Pregnant staff exposure precautions require occupational-health and facility policy.
teaching: Patients should report burning, pain, tightness, or swelling at the IV site immediately.
delegationScope: Chemotherapy administration is restricted by competency, facility, and state policy; do not assume it is within general LPN/LVN scope.
examTrap: Removing the IV catheter immediately before checking the drug-specific extravasation protocol.
oneLinePearl: Vesicant pain at the IV site = stop and follow the specific extravasation pathway.
sourceBasis: ONS antineoplastic administration and extravasation principles

title: Antibiotic Allergy vs Anaphylaxis
bottomLine: A history of nausea or diarrhea is not the same as an IgE-mediated allergy. During antibiotic therapy, hives plus airway swelling, wheeze, hypotension, or rapidly progressive multisystem symptoms indicate anaphylaxis: stop the suspected trigger, call for emergency help, and give IM epinephrine promptly per protocol.
recognize: Anaphylaxis can involve skin/mucosa, respiratory compromise, hypotension, or severe GI symptoms and may occur without a rash.
A vague childhood 'penicillin allergy' should be clarified because inaccurate labels can lead to inferior or broader-spectrum therapy.
priorities: Stop the suspected infusion/trigger while maintaining emergency access as appropriate.
Activate emergency response and assess airway, breathing, circulation.
Administer IM epinephrine as first-line treatment when anaphylaxis criteria are met.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, airway swelling, wheeze, oxygenation, skin findings, GI symptoms, and recurrence after initial improvement.
interventions: Position based on hemodynamics/breathing and provide oxygen/IV fluids as indicated.
Antihistamines are adjuncts and must not delay epinephrine.
medicationSafety: Document the reaction phenotype rather than only 'allergy' when possible.
Epinephrine is first-line for anaphylaxis; steroids and antihistamines do not replace it.
teaching: Patients with true severe allergy should know the implicated drug and reaction and carry emergency medication if prescribed.
delegationScope: Anaphylaxis recognition and emergency response require immediate licensed clinical action; do not delegate assessment of a suspected reaction.
examTrap: Giving diphenhydramine first while delaying epinephrine in true anaphylaxis.
